articles.author: Shamim Chowdhury
articles.description: Hasina's speech marked the second anniversary of her ouster. She fled Bangladesh by helicopter following nearly two months of protests in 2024 that left nearly 1,400 people dead, according to the United Nations.
articles.title: Ousted Bangladeshi leader vows to return from exile despite facing a death sentence

articles.author: Sergio Martínez-Beltrán
articles.description: The firm, Houston-based Burke Law Group has only two attorneys who specialize in immigration and asylum cases. Two of its founders have ties to the Trump administration.
articles.title: Small Texas law firm set to receive $150M to represent unaccompanied migrant children

articles.author: Pien Huang
articles.description: Schwartz takes command of a public health agency that has lost thousands of employees, amid layoffs, resignations and leadership turmoil.
articles.title: Dr. Erica Schwartz confirmed as CDC director, filling a leadership vacuum

articles.author: Raina Douris
articles.description: Morby's Little Wide Open is a love letter to a part of the country he finds endlessly inspiring.
articles.title: How Midwest doldrums became a gift for Kevin Morby

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Candidates backed by twice-elected former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League-N party have won 24 of the 34 seats decided in the first two phases of voting, the election commission, said Wednesday.
articles.title: Pakistan's ruling party leads in Kashmir vote despite boycott call by banned group

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: A 73-year-old retired nurse's decision to learn to write Tibetan language offers a glimpse into how some embrace their language and cultural identity in Tibet.
articles.title: Under China's new 'unity' law, Tibetans fight to preserve language and culture

articles.author: Maham Javaid
articles.description: El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, backs Medicare for all and decries corporate money in politics. He beat Rep. Haley Stevens, whose supporters said she would have had a better chance in the fall.
articles.title: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic primary for Senate

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Ukraine's depleted air defenses failed to stop any of Moscow's incoming missiles overnight.
articles.title: A Russian barrage in Ukraine's capital kills 17 as air defenses fall short

articles.author: Saige Miller
articles.description: Progressives notched major wins in Michigan, while voters in Missouri and Washington rejected insurgent Democrats. Meanwhile, Trump continued to flex his influence over the Republican Party.
articles.title: Progressives see biggest win yet in Michigan, while Trump flexes power over GOP

articles.author: Isabella Gomez Sarmiento
articles.description: Even as the band has changed and reinvented itself, the Grateful Dead's fanbase has proven to be uniquely and consistently renewable — a cosmic inheritance passed down from one generation to the next, welcoming younger Deadheads with open arms.
articles.title: How Deadheads became rock and roll's greatest renewable resource

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
Federal parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence continues this week. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A 60-year-old man has died after an alleged assault in Melbourne, where he was allegedly set upon by a group of youths.
Victoria police said the man sustained critical injuries on 1 August after the group of young people allegedly attempted to steal items from a nearby store in the suburb of Sunshine. The victim allegedly came to the aid of a shop employee before he was attacked himself.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: News live: Indigenous Olympian tells inquiry ‘racism, sexism, misogyny’ at Boxing Australia should be investigated

articles.author: Ben Smee and Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
A 45-year-old man and 23-year-old woman were found dead in the Charleville home after a near eight-hour police siege

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A pregnant woman and a man have been found dead at a home in the outback Queensland town of Charleville, in an apparent murder-suicide after a protracted overnight standoff with police.

 Police confirmed on Thursday that a toddler, who was found unharmed, had been at the home during the eight-hour siege that began on Wednesday evening.
Several streets in the remote town, 600km west of Toowoomba, were locked down by police after officers arrived at the property on King Street following reports of “a serious assault”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pregnant woman dead and toddler found unharmed after outback Queensland siege ends in apparent murder-suicide

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
After Ukraine failed to shoot down a single ballistic missile fired by Russia on Wednesday, the president urged allies to increase supplies of Patriot interceptors
Nato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday, and as Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Moscow was seeking to significantly boost missile ⁠production ahead of winter.
Speaking at a National Security and Defense Council meeting on winter resilience, the Ukrainian president did not rule out the idea that stalling missile supplies from western allies were “aimed at making Ukraine, so to speak, more willing to compromise” in peace talks with Russia.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nato to ‘urgently’ get air defences for Ukraine, as Zelenskyy warns of surge in Russian missile production

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Marina Dunbar and Vivian Ho
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

A quick update on the marquee Democratic primary race for US Senate in Michigan.
Haley Stevens is trailing Abdul El-Sayed by fewer than 15,000 votes, according the Associated Press, whose count the Guardian uses on election night.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan primary victory is the latest win for progressives challenging establishment-backed Democrats – as it happened

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agency
articles.description:
Jeanine John Taele faces new weapons charges as details of ‘suspicious’ behavior ahead of president’s visit emerge
A California man who was arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course ahead of a presidential visit is facing more charges, as authorities released new details about the investigation.
Authorities say federal agents first observed 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele near the golf grounds in Rancho Palos Verdes on 31 July, wearing an earpiece and capturing photographs and videos of security agents assessing the property.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man arrested at Trump’s California golf course wore earpiece and took photos, police say

articles.author: Reuters
articles.description:
Company is the third to report such an incident after Anthropic and OpenAI reported breaches during training
Meta said on Wednesday that one of its AI models hacked ⁠another company during cybersecurity testing, after an error by its testing partner gave the model unintended internet access.
The incident adds to a ⁠growing list of ⁠cases in ​which AI agents from major developers breached systems at other companies during testing, after Anthropic said last week that some of its models ⁠hacked three companies, and OpenAI disclosed that an AI agent breached the startup Hugging Face.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Meta says its AI model hacked into another company during testing

articles.author: Lucy Campbell
articles.description:
Burmese pythons are an invasive species in the Everglades, and the challenge is part of initiative to remove them
The winner of this year’s annual Florida Python Challenge hunted down and eliminated 96 invasive Burmese pythons from the Everglades national park, as part of an initiative to remove hundreds of the snakes from the area every year.
The challenge invites hunters to participate in 10 days of capturing and humanely euthanizing as many of the invasive snakes as possible across eight designated hunting locations, with the winner taking home a cash prize of $10,000. The event is hosted by Florida fish, wildlife and conservation (FWC), the south Florida water management district, the National Park Service and others.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Winner of Florida python hunting contest nabs 96 snakes: ‘I was on a mission’

articles.author: Edward Helmore
articles.description:
Variety of prescriptions were found in blood of mother accused of strangling her three children, court hears

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

The trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three children in January 2023, continued on Wednesday with a forensic toxicologist testifying to the variety and concentration of medications found in the defendant’s blood.
Justin Brower, a forensic toxicologist with NMS Laboratories, testified that his lab examined the levels of four psychiatric medications detected in Clancy’s blood after she allegedly strangled her children and attempted to take her own life.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial: toxicologist testifies about medications found in defendant’s blood

articles.author: Jonathan Barrett Business editor
articles.description:
Chief executive Robert Thomson says ‘crass kleptomaniac’ AI companies are ‘in possession of stolen goods’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

News Corp has reported a slight slide in digital subscriptions at its Australian mastheads, erasing recent gains, among otherwise robust financials at the Rupert Murdoch-backed global conglomerate.
Digital subscribers at News Corp Australia – a division that includes the Australian, the Daily Telegraph and the Herald Sun, among others – fell from 1,166,000 to 1,162,000 during the financial year, according to the company’s internal data published in its full year results on Thursday morning.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: News Corp subscriptions fall in Australia as company takes aim at ‘slimy’ AI slop

articles.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
articles.description:
Husic to take ‘short’ period of leave after collision on Sydney motorway on Tuesday

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Labor MP Ed Husic was hospitalised this week after his car was involved in an accident with a truck and another car travelling on Sydney’s M7 motorway.
The incident happened at Dean Park, as the Chifley MP was travelling home from his electorate office, around 6.20pm on Tuesday, according to a spokesperson.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labor MP Ed Husic taken to hospital with fractures and concussion after car crash

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
The 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo said
The Toronto Zoo has announced the birth of a female pygmy hippo calf.
Kindia, the zoo’s 20-year-old pygmy hippo, started showing signs of labor at around 8.15am last Sunday, it said. Around four hours later, the calf’s feet emerged and after 1.5 hours of active labor, Kindia successfully gave birth to the baby pygmy hippo.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Toronto zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother Kindia

articles.author: Deborah Cole in Berlin and Andrew Roth in Washington
articles.description:
Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt
• The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe
Germany’s interior minister has warned that the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport marks “a new level of danger” for the country, as authorities examine whether the thwarted attack could have been planned by a foreign power.
The discovery of a small drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, a leading shipping and military hub, set off alarm and caused flight diversions on Wednesday morning. German police deployed a bomb disposal robot to defuse and destroy the explosive device.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Drone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior minister

articles.author: Richard Adams and Lanre Bakare
articles.description:
Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career

Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: the claims surrounding a star Cambridge professor

Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career.
Arday, who had been dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials, issued a statement on Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarism

articles.author: Jessica Elgot, Alexandra Topping and Fiona Harvey
articles.description:
Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand

Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

The NHS has been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.
The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farming

NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper

The NHS has been told it must become more resilient to increasingly frequent heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis, as the UK government puts adaptation to extreme heat high on its agenda. But what other public services are already feeling the strain?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

articles.author: Geraldine McKelvie Senior correspondent
articles.description:
Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail
The chief constable of Thames Valley police has said he will consider joining legal action against the government if it fails to block the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.
The Police Federation is contemplating going to court in its attempts to keep Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in prison.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released early

articles.author: Lucy Campbell (now); Nadeem Badshah and Taz Ali (earlier)
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed. 
The ⁠geographic coordinates for a shipping ⁠route ⁠through the ​strait of Hormuz ⁠have been agreed by Iran and ⁠Oman, and ​a ‌joint announcement ‌is being ‌finalised, provided no third parties interfere, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei ‌said on Wednesday.
Baghaei added ​that any such agreement between Iran and ⁠Oman would not, ​by itself, ​guarantee security ​in the ​strategic waterway.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran and Oman agree on coordinates of route through strait of Hormuz, says Iranian foreign ministry – as it happened

articles.author: Andrew Roth in Washington and agencies
articles.description:
Joint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s security
Iran and Oman have reached an understanding on ⁠the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, and ⁠a joint announcement ⁠is ​being finalised provided certain third parties do not interfere, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail ⁠Baghaei said on Wednesday.
Baghaei added that any such agreement between Iran and Oman would not, by ⁠itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Understanding reached on coordinates for shipping route through Hormuz, Iran says

articles.author: Robert Tait in Washington
articles.description:
State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.
The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum

articles.author: Richard Adams and Lanre Bakare
articles.description:
University says it has ‘new information’ about academic career of Jason Arday, the youngest black professor in its history
Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, is to face investigation by the university after it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.
Cambridge initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions mounted over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cambridge announces investigation into professor accused of plagiarism

articles.author: Penelope MacRae in Delhi
articles.description:
Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students
Bangladesh’s ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence.
“They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threat

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
articles.description:
Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia
The armed drone found at Leipzig airport on Wednesday may not have exploded, but the fact that it got inside the perimeter, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, raises obvious concerns for the security of international aviation.
Though the identity of the culprits is unknown, the initial evidence points firmly towards a Russian-orchestrated plot. It is the first time that a drone with explosives has been found in Europe far from the Ukrainian border.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe

articles.author: Oscar Lopez in Mexico City
articles.description:
César Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driver
A popular Mexican influencer has been shot dead while doing a live stream on social media outside a restaurant in Sinaloa state, where lethal cartel violence has become widespread.
César Gastélum, who had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos, was filming with two friends outside a fast-food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The three were dressed in the bright orange jackets and backpacks of food delivery drivers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social media

articles.author: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad
articles.description:
Rules brought in soon after killing of dozens of protesters, news of which was reported only by overseas outlets
Pakistani authorities have imposed severe new restrictions on international media, including barring them from reporting in most of the country, in a move that has provoked a significant backlash from journalist organisations.
According to the new rules anyone, including Pakistani nationals, should seek permission first if they want to report from anywhere Pakistan except three cities – Islamabad, Karachi and Lahore.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistani authorities ban international media from reporting in most of country

articles.author: Oliver Holmes
articles.description:
Ukraine shoots down most drones but no ballistic missiles in overnight attack that mainly targeted civilian facilities
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has blamed allies for not delivering air defences fast enough after Ukraine failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in a deadly overnight attack that killed at least 17 people and ⁠injured dozens more.
Preliminary data from the Ukrainian air force showed its defences shot down 98 of the 115 drones fired by Russia overnight, but no ballistic missiles.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Zelenskyy calls for more air defences as Russian attack on Kyiv kills at least 17

articles.author: William Christou in Beirut
articles.description:
Hits on two towns among deadliest bombings since start of June ceasefire 
An Israeli airstrike in south Lebanon killed one person and injured 11, the Lebanese ministry of health said, in one of Israel’s deadliest bombings since the start of the June ceasefire.
Israel carried out an airstrike in the town of Tebnine, south Lebanon hitting a cemetery, the Lebanese health ministry said. It said the town of al-Mansouri, also in south Lebanon, was bombed too, forcing families to flee.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel strikes southern Lebanon killing one and injuring 11

articles.author: Pjotr Sauer
articles.description:
Assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory
The head of a leading Russian drone manufacturer has been critically injured in a car bomb near Ekaterinburg, in what appears to be the latest in a series of assassination attempts targeting figures linked to the country’s war in Ukraine.
Vladimir Tkachuk, the founder of the private drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, was rushed to intensive care on Wednesday after a bomb planted beneath his Mercedes exploded, according to Russian state media, citing emergency services. His bodyguard was killed in the explosion.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Head of drone manufacturer critically injured in car bomb in Russia

articles.author: Haroon Janjua in Islamabad
articles.description:
Lahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at station
The alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman with learning disabilities in a police station in Lahore, Pakistan, has prompted authorities to suspend all 78 police officers and staff at the precinct, in one of the country’s biggest ever disciplinary actions against its police force.
The woman alleges that an assistant sub-inspector apprehended her, took her to Ghaziabad police station and raped her in a room on the second floor. The woman’s family said she disappeared on the street, before returning home in tears and stating that she had been sexually assaulted at the station.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistan precinct suspends all 78 officers and staff over alleged rape at police station

articles.author: Luca Ittimani
articles.description:
New data shows the federal government scheme has been used by high-income borrowers, including one couple earning an annual $674,000

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The government’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers has enabled the purchase of nearly 1,500 properties that were turned into investments, new data shows.
The scheme is also helping hundreds of Australians earning more than $300,000 a year, after Labor stopped excluding high-income borrowers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nearly 1,500 properties bought using Australia’s first home buyers' 5% deposit scheme converted into investments

articles.author: Dan Collyns in Lima
articles.description:
Cardinal Pedro Barreto received death threats and harassment during his almost 20-year campaign against a US mining company’s operations in the Andes
A Peruvian cardinal who received a barrage of death threats when he challenged the firm behind a toxic smelter has called a $150m (£111m) out-of-court settlement to more than 1,000 people who were allegedly poisoned by the plant as children “a historic milestone”.
Cardinal Pedro Barreto, 82, was in Rome meeting Pope Leo XIV and other cardinals in June when he received news that the firm that ran the smelter, the Doe Run Company, a subsidiary of Renco Group, would pay $150m to 1,373 Peruvians who have suffered health impacts since childhood.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Peruvian cardinal hails $150m lead poisoning settlement for 1,300 people as a ‘historic milestone’

articles.author: Oscar Lopez in Mexico City
articles.description:
National Autonomous University of Mexico says applicants must take test in person after online debacle
Mexico’s largest and most prestigious university has announced that about 58,000 students will have to resit their entrance exam after abnormally high test results raised suspicions of widespread cheating.
The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam) said the exam would take place in person after its first attempt at a fully remote online version led to a debacle and thousands of annulled results.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mexico’s top university orders 58,000 students to resit entrance exam after suspected cheating

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
UN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurity
About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting.
This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices from the war in Iran.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year

articles.author: Hettie O'Brien
articles.description:
In today’s newsletter: The past week shows how quickly images, rumours and ​right-wing political opportunism can eclipse the facts on the ground
Good morning. Last week, an estimated 72,000 migrants began crossing into a tiny Spanish enclave on the tip of Morocco. Within 24 hours, most of them had headed home. At least 88 people died after attempting the crossing, according to local officials. This isn’t the whole story of what happened over the last week, but the facts are worth remembering.
At an emergency meeting yesterday, EU interior ministers sought to draw a line under Ceuta, insisting that the passport-free Schengen area had never been at risk from the arrival of migrants at this scale. Despite this, much of the media coverage has suggested that events in Ceuta represent a territorial threat to Europe, sparking calls for greater security across the region’s borders.
Environment | Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.
UK politics | Women should not feel pressurised into experiencing an “ideal birth”, the new health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has said, promising a root-and-branch reform of standards after several damning maternity scandals.
Middle East | Jordan is convening an emergency meeting over an “imminent” threat of an Israeli takeover of the most important Muslim site in Jerusalem, with the potential to “trigger a religious conflict”.
Ukraine | Russian strikes in and around Kyiv killed at least 14 people, ⁠injured 27 and ⁠damaged warehouses, ​emergency service officials said. Some reports put the death toll at 15.
Ceuta | Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wednesday briefing: ​How misinformation and ​a​ hardened immigration policy ​turned Ceuta ​into Europe’s ​latest ​flashpoint

articles.author: Ishtayaq Rasool in Indian-administered Kashmir
articles.description:
Increasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestock
As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.
“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I just want to find them’: deadly cloudbursts devastate Kashmir’s mountain communities

articles.author: Soraya Aybar Laafou in Fnideq and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid
articles.description:
People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100
Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.
Their perch was the same small tranche of land that made headlines around the world last week as extraordinary scenes emerged of about 72,000 people making their way into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
articles.description:
Snow falls in Wellington for the first time in 15 years while snow blanketed Dunedin and Christchurch on the country’s south island
Temperatures have plummeted across New Zealand as an Antarctic cold snap hovers over the country, delighting the capital, Wellington, which experienced snow for the first time in 15 years, while giving a southern city’s residents a chance to ski through the streets.
The front moved in on Tuesday, with much of the country waking to freezing conditions, frosts, snowfall, hail and bitingly cold wind.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Zealand capital delights in rare snowfall as southern city residents ski down world’s steepest street

articles.author: Natasha May in Bangkok
articles.description:
WTA event win earns 21-year-old a presidential reception in the Philippines as interest in tennis surges in home country
The Philippines has been swept up in tennis fever after 21-year-old rising star Alex Eala delivered a historic win, drawing praise from the president who hosted a reception in her honour.
On Monday, Eala became the first player from the Philippines to win a Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Tour-level singles title.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Our new champion’: Philippines swept up in tennis fever after Alex Eala’s historic win

articles.author: David Smith Washington bureau chief
articles.description:
Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília
Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud

articles.author: Lucy Campbell (now); Nadeem Badshah, Tom Ambrose and Taz Ali (earlier)
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

US and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz strait

Iran and Oman have made progress toward a deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz, a potential breakthrough that could help end the war in the Middle East, regional officials have said.
Under the emerging agreement, ships would enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a route controlled by Oman, with service fees charged for providing security and preserving the maritime environment, two regional officials told the Associated Press.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rubio hopes US can reach Hormuz deal with Iran ‘very shortly’ as officials say progress has been made – as it happened

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Masoud Pezeshkian dismisses talk of internal rift as hardline Assembly of Experts call US negotiations ‘futile’

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been forced to deny claims that he has repeatedly threatened to resign as he battles hardline factions opposed to reaching a settlement with the US over the strait of Hormuz.
The US and Europe hope a deal is imminent to reopen the strait and they are putting pressure on Oman to accept a temporary agreement that officials in Muscat fear will leave Iran retaining near permanent dominance of the vital oil shipping channel. Ships would enter the strait in a route close to Iran, but leave on a route that passes through Iranian and Omani waters.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran’s president denies threatening to resign during talks over strait of Hormuz

articles.author: Penelope MacRae in Delhi
articles.description:
Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.
Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protests

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Most of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summer
Three lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are undergoing treatment, a spokesperson said on Tuesday, as the big cats struggle in Japan’s high levels of humidity.
Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new “cruelly hot day” designation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three lions die of suspected heatstroke at Tokyo zoo as Japan swelters

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
articles.description:
Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour
A notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because it eluded trappers for three years has been caught and killed in New Zealand, ending its devastating rampage against one of the country’s rare duck populations.
The cat, a large grey tabby, is estimated to have killed dozens of New Zealand’s rarest mainland duck – or 1% of its population – plus a host of kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife during the three years it was known to be roaming the Purerua peninsula, near the top of the North Island.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three years

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Prime minister Sanae Takaichi visited Kumamoto prefecture almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 quake hit, killing 38 people
Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has visited the south-western prefecture of Kumamoto, where recovery efforts are being hampered by heat and a lack of water supplies, almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake killed dozens and caused widespread damage.
Thirty-eight people died during the quake, including one person who died of apparent heatstroke while taking shelter in a car in hot weather, officials said on Monday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Japan’s prime minister tours earthquake-hit sites as recovery efforts hampered by soaring temperatures

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.
In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Marina Dunbar and Vivian Ho
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

A quick update on the marquee Democratic primary race for US Senate in Michigan.
Haley Stevens is trailing Abdul El-Sayed by fewer than 15,000 votes, according the Associated Press, whose count the Guardian uses on election night.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan primary victory is the latest win for progressives challenging establishment-backed Democrats – as it happened

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agency
articles.description:
Jeanine John Taele faces new weapons charges as details of ‘suspicious’ behavior ahead of president’s visit emerge
A California man who was arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course ahead of a presidential visit is facing more charges, as authorities released new details about the investigation.
Authorities say federal agents first observed 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele near the golf grounds in Rancho Palos Verdes on 31 July, wearing an earpiece and capturing photographs and videos of security agents assessing the property.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man arrested at Trump’s California golf course wore earpiece and took photos, police say

articles.author: Rachel Leingang Hazel Tang John Farrell
articles.description:
Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, beat Haley Stevens to win the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan. El-Sayed will now face Republican Mike Rogers in November. Here are three major takeaways of the race from the Guardian's midwest politics correspondent Rachel Leingang
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three key takeaways from Michigan's Democratic Senate primary – video explainer

articles.author: Richard Luscombe
articles.description:
Filing by attorney general Raúl Torrez comes after DoJ appears to have ignored deadline for key Epstein ranch files
New Mexico filed a lawsuit against the US Department of Justice and the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, on Wednesday for “stonewalling” its criminal investigation into the activities of the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at a remote ranch in the state.
Raúl Torrez, the New Mexico attorney general, had said he was mulling the possibility of legal action if the justice department did not share with him by 31 July information about the alleged historical abuse of girls and young women at Epstein’s Zorro ranch about 30 miles south of Santa Fe.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Mexico sues justice department for ‘stonewalling’ Epstein investigation

articles.author: Chris Stein in Washington
articles.description:
Democrats ‘united by a common purpose: putting a check on Trump’, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand say

Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary

What we learned from midterm primary elections

Leading Democrats quickly papered over whatever qualms they had about progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed after his win in the Michigan Senate primary was confirmed on Wednesday, instead welcoming the former public health official as their champion against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers.
The state is now key to Democrats’s hopes of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. Winning in Michigan would put them on the path to snarling Donald Trump’s legislative agenda and blocking his judicial nominees for the final two years of his presidency, while defeat could undermine their prospects of gaining a majority in the chamber for years to come. Rogers lost a Senate race in Michigan two years ago by a slim margin to Democrat Elissa Slotkin.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-Sayed

articles.author: Chris Stein in Washington
articles.description:
Schwartz, president’s third pick to lead top US public health agency, confirmed in 51-44 Senate vote
Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts.
Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director

articles.author: Peter Beinart
articles.description:
The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them
Every now and then, a Senate race sets the direction for an entire party. In 1991, a state official named Harris Wofford – advised by a foul-mouthed Cajun named James Carville – upset his far better-known Republican opponent to win a special election in Pennsylvania. He did it by promising to expand access to healthcare – and thus created a template for Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign the following year.
If Abdul El-Sayed can follow up his victory in last night’s Democratic Senate primary by winning the general election in Michigan this fall, he will have created a template of his own. Despite his closer-than-expected margin of victory, his campaign offers a model for how Democrats across the country can answer the political challenge posed by Donald Trump.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism | Peter Beinart

articles.author: Norman Solomon
articles.description:
Much of the criticism of Ken Martin is deserved. But his actions are symptomatic of a party that fails to listen to the grassroots
Ken Martin is now a convenient scapegoat. As chair of the Democratic National Committee, he has stumbled into disrepute as a dubious fundraiser and bad-tempered boss who bungled an autopsy report on the 2024 election disaster. Much of the criticism is justified. But Martin is just a symptom of what deeply ails a party that does not live up to its name.
As the Democratic party’s governing body, the Democratic National Committee has long operated as a fortress for party elites who expect to get their way. Martin seemed to offer a bit of a departure when, as Minnesota party chair, he won the committee leadership election last year in part because of his close ties with other state party chairs. They remain among his strongest supporters. That’s one reason why Martin is very well-positioned to fend off any challenge to his hold on power when the full committee meets next week in Austin.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Democratic party chair is a handy scapegoat. But the party’s problems are much bigger | Norman Solomon

articles.author: Amudalat Ajasa in New York for New York Focus
articles.description:
Paraquat is banned in over 70 countries. Some farmers and their families in Hebron believe the pesticide is causing Parkinson’s disease and are demanding that New York ban it
Gordon Chaplin gingerly stepped out of the car at the top of the steep hill behind his farmhouse, sporting a bandage on his hand from a fall the day before. He gripped his cane as he shuffled through the knee-high grass. He stopped every few feet to catch his breath, leaning on his caregiver for support.
Looking out at the distant Adirondacks and Catskill mountains, he thought back to the years when he could run up the hill with ease.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The herbicide haunting a New York farm town

articles.author: Kenneth Roth
articles.description:
The administration’s proposed agreement met a scathing response. But universities must remain vigilant
The Trump administration has quietly abandoned the poisonous deal it tried to foist on American universities. Under its so-called Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education, the administration offered select universities privileged access to federal grants if they agreed to conform with Donald Trump’s ideology on how they should be run.
Universities widely pilloried the proposal, demonstrating the power of a collective defense. Higher education in the United States certainly needs reform, as many university leaders and the public would acknowledge, but not according to the dictates of Trump.
Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s university ‘compact’ is gone. That doesn’t mean the assault on education is over | Kenneth Roth

articles.author: Moustafa Bayoumi
articles.description:
Amid stop-and-start threats and with a divided staff, it’s clear Trump has no idea how to end a war that shouldn’t have begun
On Thursday, 23 July, after weeks of escalating attacks between the US and Iran, Donald Trump told a reporter that Iran hadn’t received “enough pain yet”, and he leveled a threat. “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before,” he warned. “I am close to making a decision.” Then, on Monday 27 July, he called it off.
A few days later, on Friday 31 July, Trump said: “We’ll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they’re going to say: ‘We just can’t take it any more.’” This time, it took him just one day to back down.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy | Moustafa Bayoumi

articles.author: Stephen Starr in Beavercreek, Ohio
articles.description:
Ohioans of Indian heritage will see one of their own take center stage in the race for governor, but their support amid a rocky campaign is not guaranteed
At the Hindu temple of Dayton in south-west Ohio, there’s no little pride for gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy – he and his parents have been coming here to pray for decades.
On a quiet recent Tuesday afternoon, a priest lights incense sticks at the altar of the temple. Outside, a group of first-time visitors take a relaxed walk around the grounds.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy is struggling to connect with voters. Can Ohio’s Indian community help?

articles.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman , produced by Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producers Jonathan Menjivar and Rachel Humphreys
articles.description:
Democrats are pissed off – and they're taking their anger straight to the ballot box. In the wake of Donald Trump's return to the White House, progressives (including members of DSA – Democratic Socialists of America) have defeated established moderates in elections in liberal cities like New York, Washington DC and Seattle. Now, they're trying to win a series of major primaries in the deep-purple midwest. Host Carter Sherman speaks with Guardian midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang, who has traveled all over the region covering several key races – including this week's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, where progressive Abdul Al-Sayed is squaring off against the establishment candidate, Haley Stevens. Can leftist politics win outside of blue bubbles? And what do these races reveal about the fight for the midterms and the White House?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mamdani won New York. Can a progressive win the Michigan primary? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Victoria Bekiempis
articles.description:
After the justice department botched file rollout under the original act, lawmakers now want legislation with teeth 
As Jeffrey Epstein survivors and their supporters continue searching for justice and transparency in the US, a bipartisan group of politicians is trying to rework legislation that heralded the release of long-hidden investigative files on the scandal.
While the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), signed into law by Donald Trump on 19 November, mandated that the justice department release all investigative files within 30 days with limited exceptions, survivors and their supporters have repeatedly grappled with missed deadlines and what they say are incomplete disclosures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Lawmakers push for a more robust Epstein Files Transparency Act – but would Trump sign it?

articles.author: Chris Stein in St Louis, Missouri
articles.description:
Voters face a choice of progressive ex-congresswoman Cori Bush or pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday
The pastor of a historically Black church on St Louis’s north side, Rodrick Burton, has watched with bewilderment as the congressional race in his district has drawn national attention not about the bloodshed in his community, but rather in Gaza.
“As a pastor who’s had eight members murdered, violence over there is terrible,” Burton said of the conflict in the Middle East.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will Missouri be the next primary win for a democratic socialist challenger?

articles.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman , produced by Meg Driscoll, engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Jonathan Menjivar
articles.description:
With Republicans' chances in the midterms looking shaky, Donald Trump is increasingly trying to rewrite the rules that govern US elections. Voting rights groups say he's really laying the groundwork to suppress voters. Trump has already moved to change mail-in voting, but he now wants Congress to pass the Save America Act, which includes strict voter ID restrictions. He's also accused China of interfering in the 2020 election. (Trump didn't back up that claim with evidence.) Host Kai Wright speaks with Garrett Epps, legal affairs editor at Washington Monthly, about the threat to US elections and what voters can do to protect them.

Read Garrett Epps' story in Washington Monthly

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will the US midterm elections be free and fair? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Julian Borger ; produced by Annie La Vespa and Angus Neale ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin
articles.description:
Donald Trump has declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces, but IsraelI government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal.

Lucy Hough speaks to Julian Borger, the Guardian’s senior international correspondent
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Can Trump’s Hamas disarmament plan work and will Israel agree to withdraw from Gaza? - The Latest

articles.author: Richard Adams and Lanre Bakare
articles.description:
Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career

Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: the claims surrounding a star Cambridge professor

Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career.
Arday, who had been dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials, issued a statement on Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarism

articles.author: Jessica Elgot, Alexandra Topping and Fiona Harvey
articles.description:
Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand

Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

The NHS has been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.
The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farming

NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper

The NHS has been told it must become more resilient to increasingly frequent heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis, as the UK government puts adaptation to extreme heat high on its agenda. But what other public services are already feeling the strain?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

articles.author: Geraldine McKelvie Senior correspondent
articles.description:
Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail
The chief constable of Thames Valley police has said he will consider joining legal action against the government if it fails to block the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.
The Police Federation is contemplating going to court in its attempts to keep Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in prison.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released early

articles.author: Richard Adams and Lanre Bakare
articles.description:
University says it has ‘new information’ about academic career of Jason Arday, the youngest black professor in its history
Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, is to face investigation by the university after it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.
Cambridge initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions mounted over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cambridge announces investigation into professor accused of plagiarism

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular means 
More than 1,100 people, including survivors of torture and trafficking, have been convicted of illegally arriving in the UK since 2022, according to freedom of information data.
The Home Office introduced the offence of illegal arrival in 2022 in a bid to deter those planning to come to the UK by small boat or by other irregular means such as lorries.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022

articles.author: Caroline Davies and Helena Horton
articles.description:
Metropolitan police say 47-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of possession of offensive weapon and assault
A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden, central London, police said.
The Metropolitan police said the men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to a major trauma centre after the lunchtime incident on Endell Street.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Woman arrested after four men stabbed in London’s Covent Garden

articles.author: Vivian Ho
articles.description:
Police arrested a woman in central London after four men were found with stab wounds in the shopping and entertainment district

Read the full report

Workers at the 2 Chairs Grooming Room said one of the victims ran into the shop and took his shirt off, revealing a large gash on his back.
Two of the four men stabbed this afternoon have been discharged from the hospital, the Metropolitan Police posted on X.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Woman arrested after four men stabbed in Covent Garden – as it happened

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Joshua Bonehill-Paine says Conservative leader asked him to work with party’s culture and integration commission 
A former neo-Nazi activist who was convicted of harassing a Jewish MP has withdrawn as a Conservative election candidate after Kemi Badenoch offered him a role as an adviser to the party.
Joshua Bonehill-Paine said on Wednesday that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections, and that the Conservative leader had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, where he will specifically focus on how young men become radicalised.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kemi Badenoch gives former neo-Nazi advisory role after he withdraws as Tory candidate

articles.author: Tom Ambrose (now) and Martin Belam (earlier)
articles.description:
Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council to meet with Tory party but decline meeting with Joshua Bonehill-Paine

Badenoch defends decision to allow man jailed for antisemitism to stand as councillor

Ministers will scrap the requirement for companies to prove their green and progressive values before they are awarded government contracts, and instead ask firms to prove they will help young people back into work.
As part of a government push to reduce the number of people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in the UK and boost regional growth, public sector buyers will double the consideration they give to whether companies will get more people into jobs, rather than if they can show they are improving social and environmental wellbeing. Government procurement contracts account for about £90bn of taxpayers’ money spent each year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Joshua Bonehill-Paine quits as Tory council candidate– as it happened

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
AI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk

Explainer: Should we be alarmed at AI models going rogue in tests?

Advanced artificial intelligence models have stunned the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) by carrying out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.
The institute said the incident was unprecedented and involved sending targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to try to trick developers

articles.author: Bibi van der Zee
articles.description:
Farmers advised to vaccinate after recent hot weather provides ideal conditions for virus-carrying midges
There has been an alarming surge in the number of sheep affected by an outbreak of bluetongue in the UK, and farmers whose livestock are at risk are being urged to move them out of areas where midges are plentiful.
The viral disease, which does not necessarily kill sheep but makes them ill and can have a long recovery time, presents as high fever and swelling of the lips and tongue. The tongue may go blue and even protrude from the mouth.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Alarming surge in bluetongue disease reported among UK sheep

articles.author: Jasper Jolly
articles.description:
Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first)
The taxi app company Uber and the autonomous technology developer Wayve have been granted the first minicab licences in London allowing them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now.
The companies said they would start trips in the UK “later this summer” before the full public launch.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’

articles.author: Lauren Almeida and Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Clothing and homeware retailer says growth led by suite of alternative brands and strong online sales
Next has raised hopes that UK shoppers are still willing to spend despite pressures on household budgets, after the hot summer boosted its clothing sales.
The retailer has upgraded its profit guidance for the third time this year, saying it benefited from sunny weather and the release of some “pent-up demand” in the Middle East and northern Europe in the 13 weeks ended on 1 August.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sweltering summer lifts Next sales as profit outlook upgraded again

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
Burnham said his wife, Marie-France van Heel, took some persuading after he ran and lost in contests in 2010 and 2015
Andy Burnham has revealed his wife’s dismayed reaction when he told her he wanted to make another attempt at becoming Labour leader.
Burnham said that his wife, Marie-France van Heel, had been surprised by his decision to run, having lost contests in 2010 and 2015 to Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn respectively.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Andy Burnham reveals wife’s reaction to third Labour leadership bid

articles.author: Aletha Adu Political correspondent
articles.description:
Victims’ minister said earlier that PM was ‘looking into’ inquiry into Epstein and another into Mohamed Al Fayed

Andy Burnham is not actively considering a public inquiry into the actions of Jeffrey Epstein in the UK, despite claims to the contrary.
The victims’ minister, Alex Davies-Jones, said on Tuesday that the prime minister had agreed to meet the sex offender’s victims, was “looking into” an inquiry and was “taking this very seriously”. A separate inquiry into the alleged actions of the former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed is also being considered. But the Guardian understands a public inquiry is not being actively considered by No 10.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham not considering public inquiry into UK activities of Jeffrey Epstein

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
Tory leader praises Joshua Bonehill-Paine’s ‘contrition’ but says she has higher thresholds for MP candidates

UK politics live – latest updates

Kemi Badenoch has defended her party’s decision to allow a former neo-Nazi who was jailed for subjecting a prominent Labour politician to antisemitic abuse to stand as a councillor.
Badenoch said her party was not giving Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who is standing for election in Somerset, a “national platform”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Badenoch defends decision to allow man jailed for antisemitism to stand as councillor

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Flurry of articles has raised eyebrows and drawn response from Kemi Badenoch defending stance on net zero
“Nobody can deny that the UK is getting warmer and high temperatures are becoming a clear threat to homes, nature and food security,” read the lengthy news report, which explored the devastating effect of British wildfires on families in recent years.
The article’s conclusions, written after the wildfires in Suffolk last week, were no surprise given the UK’s changing climate. However, the fact that the piece appeared in the Telegraph, the rightwing title that has been a leading critic of green policies, did raise eyebrows among some readers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Right turn on green: is the Telegraph changing its tune on the climate?

articles.author: Juliette Garside
articles.description:
Software group benefits from global systems and accounting practices ‘that enable tax to be shirked’, says union boss
The software group Palantir paid just £2m in corporation tax in the UK in 2024, despite holding public sector contracts worth hundreds of millions, thanks to tax breaks that are likely to reduce its contributions to governments around the world for years to come.
The US-headquartered company, which has harnessed AI to secure lucrative work for the NHS and the Ministry of Defence, is growing exponentially.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Palantir paid just £2m corporation tax in UK in 2024 despite lucrative public sector contracts

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Over-the-counter treatments for cats and dogs contain chemicals that are banned in pesticides and pollute waterways
Over-the-counter flea treatment for cats and dogs should be banned as millions of hazardous chemicals are unnecessarily applied to UK pets each year, a parliamentary report has concluded.
Cats and dogs are widely treated with topical, or “spot on”, treatments that include insecticides to prevent fleas. Vets often recommend regular treatments as a preventive measure, even when the animals do not have fleas.
It’s Invertebrate of the Year again! Every day from 3-12 August, we will be profiling one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and when you have heard about all of them, we will open the voting so you can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas. Email us at environment.desk@theguardian.com with Invertebrate in the subject line.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Calls to ban ‘toxic’ pet flea treatments that harm UK wildlife and environment

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
Lib Dems and many Labour MPs join farmers, landowners and firefighters in urging temporary prohibition
Farmers and landowners are calling for a temporary ban on disposable barbecues in England and Wales, as they warn of the risk of igniting wildfires.
The call, which has also been made by firefighters and is backed by the Liberal Democrats and many Labour MPs, comes as much of England faces further hot dry weather, despite rain in some areas.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Calls to ban disposable barbecues in England and Wales over wildfire risk

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
John Barstow says oil expansion is a necessity, while David Parker wonders if the prime minister will protect the planet or the fossil fuel industry
North Sea oil expansion is a necessity (Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling, 31 July). I state this as an environmentalist – not despite. Oil is a feedstock, not mere fuel. Oil is necessary for the day-to-day maintenance of wind turbines, nuclear plants and rail. Hence oil is part and parcel of supply chains for green tech. A domestic oil base brings such supply chains closer. This also underscores the case for approval of coking coal extraction in Cumbria. Green tech needs high-grade steel and high-grade steel needs coking coal.
There are much better ways of helping the environment, such as more tree planting and stopping plastic waste being dumped into our seas. The carbon sink factor would be helped. A major expansion of the UK’s North Sea oil sector will make a more cohesive UK, complete with more jobs in Scotland and the north of England, including in supply manufacturing chains.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: North Sea oil is a litmus test for Burnham | Letters

articles.author: Emma Loffhagen
articles.description:
Poetry sales surpassed £8m in the first 30 weeks of 2026 and are expected to reach a record high this year thanks to blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s 2,700-year-old poem

UK poetry sales are on course to reach a record high this year, buoyed by the success of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of Homer’s The Odyssey.
Poetry sales surpassed £8m during the first 30 weeks of 2026, an increase of 13.3% on the same period last year, according to data from market researchers NielsenIQ.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey gives UK poetry sales an epic boost

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
Rhys Ifans, Matthew Rhys, Aimee-Ffion Edwards and Mark Lewis Jones among actors voicing characters from 1977 blockbuster
There are a few links between the Star Wars franchise and Wales, including the secretive building of the Millennium Falcon in an old hangar in the far south-west of the Celtic nation.
But until now, speakers of Welsh – Cymraeg – have not been able to hear the words of Luke Skywalker, Han Solo and Princess Leia spoken in their own language.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Star Wars dubbed into Welsh for first time for S4C broadcast

articles.author: Mark Fisher
articles.description:
Beginning his career as an actor, Gill went on to write plays including The York Realist as well as directing for the Royal Court and National Theatre
Tributes have been paid to the director and playwright Peter Gill who died on Monday at the age of 86. His agent Mel Kenyon said Gill’s work had a “rare emotional delicacy” and was “beautifully observed and finely tuned” while the director Michael Grandage said Gill’s “contribution to the British theatre will come to be regarded as quietly seismic”.
Gill began his career as an actor at London’s Royal Court in 1958 when still in his teens. Over the next six years, he played Silvius opposite Vanessa Redgrave as Rosalind in Michael Elliott’s lauded RSC production of As You Like It, as well as several roles in the British premiere of Brecht’s The Caucasian Chalk Circle.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Peter Gill, playwright who turned ordinary lives into extraordinary drama, dies aged 86

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
After a blitz of small wins, PM is finding that like Keir Starmer there is only so much he can control on the big calls
If Andy Burnham wanted to demonstrate he was the anti-Keir Starmer, the first fortnight could not have gone better. Instead of painting a gloomy picture of tough times and an economic black hole that would only improve with sacrifices such as cutting winter fuel allowance, Burnham’s first week was a blitz of small wins including cutting bus fares.
But the new prime minister can only control so much. And like Starmer, within his first days in office he found himself facing immediate decisions where every call will make you unpopular. And – like Starmer – blaming your predecessor counts for nothing with an angry public.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler and Amee Joshi
articles.description:
This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways
The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side.
Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train

articles.author: Presented and produced by Madeleine Finlay, sound design by Joel Cox, the executive producer was Ellie Bury
articles.description:
Madeleine Finlay travels to the Rothbury estate in Northumberland, in north-east England. It’s a piece of land that has been in the same family for 700 years, but now it has been put up for sale and the UK’s Wildlife Trusts are trying to raise £30m to secure it intact. To find out what makes the area so special, Madeleine speaks to Katy Barke, the head of nature recovery for Northumberland Wildlife Trust. She also hears from Sam Turner, a professor of archaeology at Newcastle University, who is trying to work out how the land has been used across the centuries. This work will inform the strategy for nature recovery on the site. And Rosie Pearce, a farm liaison officer, explains how the project could bring more wildlife-friendly farming practices to the estate

Northumberland nature recovery project takes shape with biggest land sale in 30 years
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The fight to save a historic English landscape - podcast

articles.author: Hettie O'Brien
articles.description:
In today’s newsletter: A small chorus of right-leaning critics are trying to convince politicians that climate action is deeply unpopular, downplaying its seriousness in the process
Good morning. Half of England and all of Wales are officially in drought, wildfires have burned through parts of the Cairngorms, Suffolk and the Isle of Wight, and reservoirs are running low. Farmers have warned that there could soon be food shortages, and the Royal Horticultural Society is considering moving its hydrangeas to cope with the heat. Many people are now asking a question rarely associated with British summertime: when will it rain?
The Guardian has been covering how the climate crisis is supercharging wildfires in Europe, the impossible choices firefighters face about which places to save, the numb…
articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Inside the right’s heated climate-denial debate

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Findings prompt calls for review of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence criteria in women under 50
Young women in England who later develop breast cancer are not being referred for early tests or preventive treatment because current guidelines used by GPs miss 95% of patients, research suggests.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) criteria used to decide who should be referred by family doctors for further breast cancer risk assessment and specialist care is failing to spot the vast majority of women under 50 who will go on to develop the disease in the next 10 years, according to the University of Cambridge and the Institute of Cancer Research, London (ICR).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: GPs’ breast cancer guidelines ‘miss’ 95% of young women who will develop disease

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Anna Isaac; produced by Natalie Ktena, Eleanor Biggs, Saskia Collette, Nilufer Aumeerally and Ross Burns; executive producers Sami Kent and Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
Reform UK’s finances have come under scrutiny like never before. What do we know about the party’s funding – and why do so many awkward questions remain for Nigel Farage? Anna Isaac explains
For a while this year, it looked like nothing could stop Nigel Farage getting to Downing Street. Not the allegations of schoolboy racism, not the dodgy Cameo videos or even the £400,000 he trousered for advertising gold bullion.
But at the end of April, the Guardian’s City editor, Anna Isaac, delivered a game-changing scoop. That Farage had been given a £5m gift, as he termed it, from the cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harbourne.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nigel Farage and the £5m question that won’t go away – podcast

articles.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
articles.description:
Survey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staff
NHS radiographers are experiencing racist abuse by patients, who have called them “monkeys” and refused to be seen by black and Asian staff, according to a report.
A survey of 381 members of the Society of Radiographers revealed a “noticeable” rise in instances of overt racism experienced and witnessed by radiographers across the health service over the past 18 months.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS radiographers report rise in overt racist abuse by patients

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Restore leader has countered charges he’s splitting the right while showing his party is a very real obstacle for Reform
Even by the standards of their rivalry, the speed at which Rupert Lowe’s olive branch to Nigel Farage morphed into fresh recriminations between the two was swift.
It began with a softly lit 12-minute video posted on Sunday by the Restore Britain leader, looking straight to camera and referring to “Nigel” as he suggested his party could be willing to cast aside its differences with Reform UK and work together.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rupert Lowe’s ‘olive branch’ to Farage piles more pressure on Reform leader

articles.author: Rajeev Syal and Dan Sabbagh
articles.description:
Nigel Farage says he would use the military in the Channel but there are questions about whether the plan would work
